approachQuestion.prompt:
Occupied platforms. There are n numbered platforms initially empty. Each of m reservations occupies every platform from l through r inclusive once. Return how many platforms have occupancy at least t after all reservations.

Input: n=5, reservations [[0,2],[1,3],[3,4]], t=2. Output: 3.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n,m ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ t ≤ m; 0 ≤ l ≤ r < n. Reservations may repeat.

Which approach handles the complete task correctly and efficiently?

options.text: Allocate n+1 zero events. Add 1 at each l and -1 at each r+1. Scan the first n events, tracking occupancy and counting positions where it is at least t.
options.feedback: Events combine every reservation, including repeats. The running sum is the occupancy of the current platform.

options.text: Count the number of reservation pairs that overlap and return it.
options.feedback: For n=3, reservations [[0,2],[0,2]], t=2, there is one intersecting pair but three qualifying platforms.

options.text: Increment all positions in each reservation, then count those at least t.
options.feedback: This gives correct results, but repeatedly traverses overlapping candidates. The selected summary reuses their shared work.

feedback.reason: Allocate n+1 zero events. Add 1 at each l and -1 at each r+1. Scan the first n events, tracking occupancy and counting positions where it is at least t.
details: Allocate n+1 zero events. Add 1 at each l and -1 at each r+1. Scan the first n events, tracking occupancy and counting positions where it is at least t.

Record reservation start and one-past-end events, then inspect occupancy after applying each platform's event. Duplicate reservations contribute independently. Thresholding events directly would confuse changes with accumulated occupancy.

“Allocate n+1 zero events. Add 1 at each l and -1 at each r+1. Scan the first n events, tracking occupancy and counting positions where it is at least t.”: Events combine every reservation, including repeats. The running sum is the occupancy of the current platform.
“Count the number of reservation pairs that overlap and return it.”: For n=3, reservations [[0,2],[0,2]], t=2, there is one intersecting pair but three qualifying platforms.

“Increment all positions in each reservation, then count those at least t.”: This gives correct results, but repeatedly traverses overlapping candidates. The selected summary reuses their shared work.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the method in the reveal. Choose its tightest worst-case time and worst-case auxiliary-space pair. Use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Exclude read-only input and required output; include every described table. All loops are iterative, with no recursive stack or input copies.

options.text: O(n + m) time; O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + m) time; O(1) auxiliary space
O(n log n + m) time; O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Process m boundary pairs and n reconstructed occupancy values.
details: Initialize n+1 events and process m reservations then n platforms. Events require O(n) space; result is scalar.
Use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Exclude read-only input and required output; include every described table. All loops are iterative, with no recursive stack or input copies.

Initialize n+1 event slots, perform two boundary updates for each of m reservations, then scan n platforms once. With constant-time indexed 64-bit operations, total time is O(n+m). O(nm) would revisit every covered platform for every reservation. O(n log n+m) adds sorting or tree operations absent from the indexed event-array method.

The event array has n+1 live entries, and occupancy, qualifying-platform count, and indices are scalars, so auxiliary space is O(n). The O(1)-space choice drops the event array. Reservations are supplied input and the returned count is a scalar; neither exclusion removes the separate event storage.
